messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding, Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body, Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Negative Appraisals: Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Martin Weber is a 66-year-old software engineer who came to treatment after years of living around reactions he rarely spoke about, even to his wife. He grew up in the Midwest in a family that prized self-control and privacy, and when he describes his childhood he does so sparingly, as if each detail has to be handled with care. The central trauma he returns to is repeated physical abuse by a caregiver in the home. What stands out in his account is not only being hit, but the way it arrived without warning. He remembers being approached from behind or having a hand suddenly clamp onto his arm or shoulder before he had even turned around. He remembers the coldness of a room or the feel of temperature on his skin just before contact, and the immediate pounding in his chest as he tried to gauge what was coming. In his memory, ordinary objects in the house were never just ordinary; anything within reach could become dangerous. Even now, when the memory flashes up suddenly, it comes with that same sense that harm can materialize out of whatever is nearby.

For decades Martin built a life that, from the outside, looked stable. He married, developed a long career in software engineering, and became known at work as precise, reliable, and somewhat private. But he had come to believe that safety depended on being especially careful because “you never know what can happen next.” He scans rooms automatically for objects that could be used as weapons or for anything hard, sharp, or heavy enough to do damage. In conference rooms he notices the letter opener, the metal water bottle, the heavy stapler. In restaurants he clocks the steak knives before he has settled into his seat. He does not describe this as a choice so much as something his body does first, before he has had time to think. If a colleague brushes past him unexpectedly in a crowded hallway, he jolts violently, heart hammering, ashamed to find himself reacting before he knows why.

His body has become, in his mind, an unsafe place to pay attention to. A sudden pounding heart is one of the most potent cues. If he notices it after climbing stairs, during an argument, or even after rushing to make a meeting, he can feel himself pulled toward the old scenes. The memory does not unfold as a calm recollection; it intrudes abruptly, and with it comes the same certainty of danger. Certain temperatures on his skin can do the same. A chill in an over-air-conditioned office, stepping into a cold room, or the particular cool touch of air on his forearms can stop him in place for a moment, as if he has been dropped back into childhood before his mind catches up.

Over time Martin narrowed his life in ways that made sense to him. He stopped paying attention to his body whenever possible. He avoids looking at himself closely, does not linger over bodily sensations, and turns away from anything that would make him too aware of his physical self. He also avoids touch. His wife has learned, painfully, that even affectionate contact can unsettle him if it is not expected. He pulls away from casual pats on the back, stiffens when someone reaches for his shoulder, and prefers to position himself where no one can come up behind him. At work he has long favored remote communication, framing it as efficiency, but in person he keeps distance and avoids the loose social contact that others take for granted.

He also withdrew from people he had socialized with before the abuse, or who belonged to that earlier world. Over the years reunions, old family gatherings, and contact with longstanding acquaintances came to feel intolerable. He could not shake the sense that other people were fundamentally untrustworthy and that he himself was somehow permanently set apart from them, an outsider who would never move through relationships with the same ease others seemed to have. Those beliefs have made his world lonelier, though he speaks of the loneliness almost as a cost of staying safe.

What finally brought him in was not a single crisis but an accumulation. Recently, an unexpected touch at work triggered such a strong alarm response that a younger coworker asked if he was all right, and Martin found himself unable to answer. Around the same time, his wife told him she felt she had to “announce” every gesture in their home, as if she were living around a perimeter. He was shaken by how normal that had come to seem. Now, seeking help in his mid-sixties, Martin says he is tired of living as though danger is always one second away, but he is equally afraid that lowering his guard would be naive. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to become a different person, but to have his own body, his marriage, and ordinary rooms feel less like places where anything might suddenly turn.
